echoes.note: "Christ suffered for us in the flesh" (4:1) reprises the Suffering Servant who suffered/bore in his body, the controlling christological frame of 1 Peter (cf. 2:21-25). Sets up the believer's call to share that mindset.
"Arm yourselves" (hoplisasthe, 4:1) may echo the divine warrior who puts on righteousness/salvation as armor; the military arming metaphor recurs in early Christian paraenesis. Faint and disputed.

The vice catalog of 4:3 (lewdness, drunken binges, orgies, "abominable idolatries") follows the Hellenistic-Jewish topos that Gentile idolatry breeds sexual and social corruption, classically developed in Wisdom's indictment of idol-worship. Deuterocanonical.

"Abominable idolatries" (4:3) and the catalog of "desire of the Gentiles" recall the Holiness Code's warning against the abominations of the nations that defile the land; shared abomination-of-the-Gentiles framing. Thematic, contested.
Drunkenness, whoredom, and idolatry chained together as the religion of the nations parallels the moral logic of the 4:3 vice list. Faint.
God "ready to judge the living and the dead" (4:5) draws on the OT confession that the LORD comes to judge the earth/the peoples; cf. Psalm 98:9. Generic judgment-theophany echo.
"Him who is ready to judge" (4:5) reflects the standing title of God as Judge of all the earth who renders account. Faint topical echo.

"The end of all things is near" (4:7) strongly recalls Ezekiel's emphatic oracle, "An end! The end has come... the end is upon you," the prophetic announcement of imminent eschatological judgment. Shared end (telos) language and nearness.

"Love covers a multitude of sins" (4:8) verbatim-quotes Proverbs 10:12 ("love covers all transgressions"), closer to the Hebrew/proverbial sense than LXX. Foundational maxim of the pericope; cf. James 5:20.
The call to hospitality (4:9) and stewardship of gifts toward one another resonates with the prophetic ideal of sharing bread and shelter with the needy. Thematic, faint.
"He who covers a transgression seeks love" offers a near-parallel proverb to 4:8, reinforcing the love-covers-sin tradition; possible secondary source alongside Proverbs 10:12.
The "fiery trial... to test you" (4:12) draws on the wisdom/prophetic metaphor of the crucible refining metal as God tests his people; cf. the smelting imagery the verse shares with Proverbs 17:3.
The refining fire that purifies (4:12) echoes the Lord's coming as a refiner's fire who purges the sons of Levi; this same Malachi context (judgment beginning at the temple) also feeds 4:17.

"I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and try them as gold" closely parallels the testing-by-fire of God's remnant in 4:12. Strong thematic and verbal coherence.
"You, God, have tested us; you have refined us as silver is refined" supplies the same trial-as-refining figure behind 4:12. Faint, one of several refining texts.

"The Spirit of glory and of God rests on you" (4:14) reworks "the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him" (the messianic endowment), transferring the resting Spirit from the Messiah to the reproached believer. Verbal "rests/Spirit" link.
Being "insulted for the name of Christ" (4:14) evokes the psalmist bearing the reproach of God's servants and of the LORD's anointed; shared reproach-for-the-name motif. Cf. Psalm 69:9.

"Judgment to begin with the household of God" (4:17) draws directly on the command to begin the slaughter "at my sanctuary," i.e., judgment commencing with God's own house before the wider world. Core source for the verse's logic.

"I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should you go utterly unpunished?" supplies the a fortiori structure of 4:17 (if it begins with us, what of the disobedient?). Strong conceptual parallel.
The Lord suddenly coming to his temple to judge begins purifying judgment at the house of God (4:17), reinforcing Ezekiel 9; the same passage's refining fire underlies 4:12.
"You only have I known... therefore I will punish you" expresses the same principle that election intensifies rather than exempts from judgment, undergirding 4:17. Thematic.

"If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?" (4:18) cites Proverbs 11:31 in its LXX form verbatim (the LXX renders the Hebrew as a saved/scarcely-saved a fortiori). Formula-cited proverb.

"Entrust their souls to him" (4:19) echoes "Into your hand I commit my spirit," the psalm of committing oneself to God amid suffering (also on Christ's lips, Luke 23:46). Verbal commit-to-God parallel.
"A faithful Creator" (4:19) draws on the prophetic confession of God as the faithful Creator and Redeemer of his people who can be trusted in trial. Faint, supports the entrusting-to-Creator theme.
